To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the distribution of voltage-dependent Na(+) channels identified by high affinity receptors for tetrodo-toxin and saxitoxic in rat and human brain were quantitatively analyzed using light microscopic autoradiography with tritiated derivatives of tetrodotoxic and saxitoxic.

(i) the distribution of tetrodoxin and saxitoxins binding sites in the rat brain is similar to that of the Na+ channel protein and (ii) the distribution of the binding sites for these toxins in the human brain is similar to the distribution of the Na+ channels.

the distribution of voltage-dependent Na channels identified by high affinity binding sites for tetrodoxin and saxitoxins in rat and human brain is very heterogeneous and that the distribution of the Na channels in human brain is very similar to that in rat brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the localization of a voltage-dependent Na+ conductance in the adult brain, which is the target for tetrodtoxin and saxitaxin.
the localization and quantitation of a Na+ channel in rat and human brain.
the identification of the voltage-dependent Na+ conductance in rat and human brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tetrodotoxins and saxitoxins bind to a single class of high affinity sites which correspond to a putative voltage-sensitive Na+ channel.
the Na+ channel receptor for saxitoxin and tetrodotoxins is widely distributed throughout the central nervous system.
tetrodotoxine and saxitoxine binding sites are present in all rat and human brain regions, with a particularly high density in the cerebral cortex, hippocampal formation and cerebellum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distribution of voltage-dependent Na channels is heterogeneous in the brain.
the voltage-dependent Na+ (Na+) channel identified by high-affinities for tetrodotoroxin and saxitoxins is present in all brain structures.
the Na+ channel is present in the majority of brain regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
voltage-dependent Na+ (Na(v)) channels are widely expressed in the central nervous system.
the distribution of Na+ channels is not uniform throughout the rat or human brain.
the Na+ channel distribution in the rat and human brain appears to be quite similar, which is in agreement with the hypothesis that these receptors are part of a single Na+ channel protein.
